The case chosen for this study is the rotor blade of Garrett's TFE 731-2 high pressure turbine.
Experimental measurements of tip and shroud heat transfer for this turbine were available from previous studies.
The Baldwin and Lomax algebraic turbulence model was used, with the Prandtl-Van Driest formulation for the inner layer.
Transition was modeled using the method described by Mayle (1991).
The computations were performed using a multi-block grid system with five blocks, including C-grids, an O-grid, and an H-grid.
Placing the inlet boundary at 30% of axial chord upstream of the leading edge with a 0.1% inlet boundary layer thickness resulted in better agreement with experimental data.
Increasing the rotation rate slightly increased the heat transfer on the blade tip leading edge region, but had minimal effect on the shroud heat transfer.
Regions of large heat transfer rates were identified close to the leading edge of the blade tip and along the edge on the suction side.
The average shroud heat transfer decreased monotonically with increasing distance along the axial flow direction.
Increasing the tip clearance gap size from 1.1% to 1.8% of span resulted in a general decline in the tip heat transfer levels.
Accurate prediction of tip heat transfer required at least 40 cells in the radial direction within the small tip clearance region.
Differences between simulations and experiments were attributed to simplified inlet boundary conditions and the absence of the shroud recess in the computational model.
The study provided insights into the dominant flow and heat transfer mechanisms affecting the blade tip and shroud regions.
The computational approach used in this study can be applied to other turbine blade designs to predict tip and shroud heat transfer.
The results of this study can inform the design of cooling schemes and clearance gap control for gas turbine engines.
